evidence.sectionTitle: Salvation, sincere seeking, and explicit belief

card.critique: Strongest feature: Sechler distinguishes moral decency from truth-directed effort to serve God, clarifying that his inclusivism retains a Christian condition while answering Clifton’s concern about salvation depending upon theology. Principal limitation: The 57 evidential-warrant score reflects that sincere truth-seeking does not demonstrate an unconvinced seeker is knowingly serving God, and the account risks redescribing involuntary nonbelief as inadequate pursuit without explaining recognition. Live burden: Sechler needs to explain how divine justice reliably identifies God-directed seeking among people who conscientiously investigate yet remain unable to believe, without quietly restoring the disputed propositional-belief requirement under different terminology. Locked score: 71 reflects a responsive refinement whose distinction improves the proposal, while its treatment of blameless nonrecognition remains insufficiently established.

card.critique: Strongest feature: Clifton tests Sechler’s inclusivism by arguing that annihilation deprives an involuntary nonbeliever of salvation’s infinite benefit, so changing the consequence from punishment to nonreward does not remove the justice problem; this reply supports responsiveness at 90. Principal limitation: The 70 evidential-warrant score reflects that Clifton calls the deprivation unjust without defending why salvation is an entitlement rather than a gift, especially if annihilation involves no suffering. Live burden: Clifton needs to establish which principle makes withholding an infinite benefit wrongful when the belief is theologically uncompelled, and why that principle survives the punishment-versus-nonreward distinction. Locked score: 84 fits a relevant challenge that exposes the stakes of involuntary belief while leaving its account of deserved benefits incomplete.
